sections.h2: Who sends and collects property tax bills in Jackson County, Michigan?
sections.html:
Your city or township sends and collects the bill first, and the Jackson County Treasurer takes over only when taxes go delinquent. That split catches many sellers off guard, because the County Treasurer's office is not where you pay a current bill. A homeowner who is current pays the local unit. An owner who has fallen behind pays the County Treasurer's Office instead.

Jackson County covers about 702 square miles of land and has a single city, Jackson, which is also the county seat. Brooklyn, Cement City (partly in the county), Concord, Grass Lake, Hanover, Parma and Springport are villages, and the rest of the county is organized into townships. Each of those local units bills its own residents, so the first step when you plan to sell is to find out which unit bills your parcel.

sections.h2: What is the Jackson County property tax calendar?
sections.html:
Every Jackson County owner gets a summer bill in July and a winter bill in December. The dates below are recurring rules from the county's Current Tax Cycle page, and the City of Jackson runs a slightly different schedule from the townships.

Jackson County tax calendar
EventTownships and villagesCity of Jackson
Summer bill issuedJulyJuly
Summer paymentPenalty after September 14; interest of 1 percent a month from September 15Pay in full by July 31, or in 5 installments due on the 20th of each month from July through November
Winter bill issuedDecemberPayable in full December 1 through February 14
Winter payment dueFebruary 14, with added penalties February 15 to 28February 14
DelinquentAnything unpaid after the last day of February goes to the County TreasurerSame

Source: Jackson County, Current Tax Cycle. Contact your township for its own penalty policy, and notify your local unit if a bill never arrives, because the county says that duty rests with the owner.

sections.h2: What happens when a Jackson County tax bill becomes delinquent?
sections.html:
A delinquent bill is forwarded to the County Treasurer for collection, and every payment on it must then go to that office. The county adds a 4 percent penalty and 1 percent interest in the first month of delinquency, then 1 percent for each month after. Taxes that stay unpaid longer than one year attract a higher interest rate and added fees.

The Treasurer also acts as collector of delinquent personal property taxes for 18 units and administers the Delinquent Tax Revolving Fund, which lets local units, schools and the junior college keep full use of their levies while the county chases the unpaid balance. For real estate, the office conducts an annual tax sale of properties delinquent three or more years. A seller sitting on three years of unpaid tax has far fewer options than one who is a few months behind, so sell before the clock gets that far.

sections.h2: How do I pay delinquent taxes to the Jackson County Treasurer?
sections.html:
The Treasurer's Office is at 120 W. Michigan Avenue, first floor, Jackson, MI 49201, and the main number is 517-788-4418. It accepts cash, check, money order or credit card. Pick whichever of these fits your timing:

  • By phone, at (855) 246-9331 (toll-free). Have your parcel ID ready; the call carries a 3 percent convenience fee with a $2.00 minimum.
  • Online with a credit card, at a 3 percent convenience fee.
  • In person at the Treasurer's Office.
  • By mail, with a check payable to the Jackson County Treasurer that lists the parcel ID and the tax years being paid.

Call 517-788-4418 for an exact payoff before mailing a check. The county notes that a check refused by the bank puts the tax back on the roll as unpaid, with all interest and penalties restored. If you do not know your parcel ID, your township or city office can supply it, and so can the county GIS parcel viewer.

sections.h2: Does a Jackson County deed need a tax certification?
sections.html:
Yes, for warranty deeds. The Treasurer's principal duties include certifying warranty deeds, and Michigan law requires that certification before such a deed is recorded. The same step applies to other documents carrying a covenant of warranty under Michigan law, so ask your closing agent to order the certification early.

If you owe delinquent tax on the parcel, expect the certification and the closing to run through the Treasurer's payoff figure. You can request that figure by phone at 517-788-4418 before closing day.

sections.h2: How do I look up my Jackson County property record?
sections.html:
Jackson County runs its records on BS&A Online. You can search by address, owner name or parcel number, pull an assessing record, check a property sale search, look up delinquent tax records, and pay delinquent taxes. A resident account lets you claim up to five properties at no charge.

Pull up your assessing record before you list. It shows what your local assessor has on file for the house. If the figures look wrong, the city or township assessor is the person to ask, since most Michigan assessing is local rather than county.

sections.h2: What do the numbers say about Jackson County homes?
sections.html:
Jackson County is the biggest of the four Michigan counties in this set. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table gives 159,552 people in July 2025 and 69,801 housing units, with 21.5 percent of residents aged 65 or older. About 75.0 percent of homes are owner-occupied, and the median value is $193,700 for 2020 to 2024. Median gross rent is $985, the highest of the four counties, and median household income is $66,073. Builders took out 303 permits in 2025.

I-94 and US-127 both cross the county, along with M-50, M-52, M-60, M-99 and M-106, and the mean commute is 22.5 minutes. The Grand River runs through the city of Jackson, and the 21,000-acre Waterloo State Recreation Area sits in the east of the county.

sections.h2: How does selling change the next Jackson County tax bill?
sections.html:
A sale resets the tax cap. Michigan Treasury says a transfer of ownership uncaps taxable value in the calendar year after the transfer, so a buyer should expect the bill to move toward the assessed value. The buyer files a Property Transfer Affidavit (Form 2766) with the local assessor, and transfers that are exempt from uncapping are listed in section 211.27a(7) of the General Property Tax Act.

Because the summer bill and the winter bill land on different local deadlines, ask your closing agent to prorate current taxes on the settlement statement.

faqs.q: When does a Jackson County property tax bill become delinquent?
faqs.a: Any amount unpaid by the last day of February is delinquent and goes to the County Treasurer. A 4 percent penalty and 1 percent interest apply in the first month, then 1 percent monthly.

faqs.q: Is the Jackson County Treasurer where I pay my regular summer or winter bill?
faqs.a: No. Current bills are paid to your city or township, and the Treasurer's Office handles delinquent ones. The City of Jackson has its own deadlines, with the summer bill due by July 31 or in five installments.

faqs.q: How can I pay a delinquent tax by phone in Jackson County?
faqs.a: Call (855) 246-9331 with your parcel ID. A 3 percent convenience fee applies, with a $2.00 minimum. Online card payments carry the same 3 percent fee.

faqs.q: What if my Jackson County tax bill never arrives?
faqs.a: The county says it is your responsibility as owner to tell your local township or city that you did not get a bill. Contact that office promptly, since missing a bill does not stop penalties.

faqs.q: Does Jackson County sell homes for unpaid taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The County Treasurer conducts an annual tax sale of real estate that has been delinquent for three or more years. Contact the Treasurer on 517-788-4418 about your parcel before it reaches that point.
